title: Tailscale MCP Servers Explained: One Exposed Tool Server
summary: Tailscale MCP servers run on private tailnet addresses only enrolled devices can access. Understand how this differs from standard MCP deployments.
body_markdown:
## Tailnet controls who, not what


Nothing stopped it at the network, because the tailnet controls who can reach the server, not what they may do once connected.


Of the 26,548 MCP hosts[Spellwarden](https://spellwarden.ai/research/mcp-server-security-2026-11.pdf) examined, **16,470 needed no sign-in** , and 9,691 exposed write-capable tools. So about 62% let anyone list their tools, and more than a third could change something, so attackers could map and modify most systems.


Five causes explain how a private network ends up in that position:


- **A private network is not authorisation** .
- The access rule allows all by default.
- A contractor laptop carries no tag.
- One broad database credential sits behind the server.
- Nothing limits each tool to read or write.


Under Tailscale's default access rule, every device can reach every other. An untagged contractor laptop therefore arrives with the same reach as an engineer's workstation, and the server can't tell them apart.


Tags and a narrowed rule are what turn "on the network" into "allowed to call this tool."


An agent built on a bare SDK has code to run but no role and no audit trail, and Activepieces treats it as a user instead: RBAC, SSO and SCIM govern which connections it may use, the same model that governs your staff, and the enterprise RBAC documentation sets out access policies that apply to what an agent may connect to, not just what a person may open.


Its run detail view lists every tool call within an agent step as a separate entry, each with its own input and output, rather than one opaque result. MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run Activepieces in production.


It only earns a place if agent calls should run approved workflows over MCP.


### One credential behind every tool


In 7.8% of MCP server builds,[Island](https://www.island.io/blog/your-ai-can-be-given-secret-instructions-in-plain-english) found code execution, and in 40.6% a tool touching sensitive data, meaning nearly half the examined builds lacked adequate isolation from either uncontrolled code execution or unguarded data access.


A build with either capability is one whose credential deserves the closest scrutiny.


The same research found **92% of builds carried no organisational signal** , meaning nothing in the build shows who owns it or whether anyone approved it.


Put one broad database login behind such a server and every connected device inherits the whole database. Give each tool its own credential, limited to read or write on the tables it needs, and a stolen session loses most of its value.


### Serve and Funnel confused in setup


Get the two mixed up during setup and a private server becomes a public one without any visible error. Tailscale Serve publishes a service to the tailnet only. Funnel publishes it to the public internet. Confirm which was used before anything else is checked.
